why: Evidence: (1) Zero errors everywhere - stable 0 5xx / 7343 reqs and canary 0 5xx / 2476 reqs, 0.00% err on /browse, /search and /checkout, and 0 5xx in all four 30s windows. No correctness or availability signal against 1.1. (2) The latency gap is a warm-up transient, not a regression. The over-time table shows canary p95 at 210ms (0-30s), 130ms (30-60s), 95ms (60-90s), 94ms (90-120s), while stable p95 is flat at 93/94/95/94ms. The canary converges to stable parity by the 60s mark and stays there for the final 60s - the last two windows are within 1ms of stable. (3) The scary aggregate numbers (canary p95 177ms vs stable 94ms; /browse 150 vs 27; /search 177 vs 59; /checkout 215 vs 103) are whole-test aggregates, so they are dominated by the first 60s of warm-up. They describe a cold pod, not the pod's steady state. Judgement: a single freshly started pod paying JIT/cold-cache/connection-pool costs for its first ~60s under load is expected behaviour, and the steady-state evidence (parity at p95, zero errors, including on the revenue path /checkout) is the right basis for the promote/rollback call. Rolling back here would block a release over a startup cost that the data shows already resolved. Judgement / caveat not provable from this dashboard: the aggregate p50 gap (62ms vs 34ms) is larger than I would expect from a 25%-of-requests warm-up window alone, and the over-time table only reports p95, so steady-state p50 parity is inferred rather than measured. Recommended guard rails on promote: roll out gradually (surge a few pods at a time, not all at once) so each new 1.1 pod's warm-up window is absorbed by already-warm pods; make the readiness probe gate on a warmed state so cold pods do not take traffic; and watch p95 and 5xx on /checkout through the rollout, reverting if p95 stays above ~110ms after a pod has been serving for more than 60s or if any 5xx appear.
